1.title: Security Operations: Monitoring, Triage, Threat Actors and Frameworks
1.text: Welcome to Module fourteen: Security Operations: Monitoring, Triage, Threat Actors and Frameworks. It covers the exam area five. Security Operations and Incident Response. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. five point two Understand security operations: Logging and monitoring security events. Security event triage (for example incident use cases, prioritization, correlation). Threat actors (for example types, motivations). Cyber threat intelligence. Threat frameworks. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: five. Security Operations and Incident Response (seventeen point three percent). Exam format: an adaptive exam of one hundred to one hundred twenty-five questions in two hours; a score of seven hundred on a scale of one to one thousand passes. Validated against: the official I S C two C C exam outline.

1.title: Logging and monitoring
1.text: Logging and monitoring. A security operations center (sock) watches, detects and responds to security events around the clock.

1.title: Logging and monitoring, continued
1.text: Logging and monitoring. The figure shows this: From logs to alerts to triage: the security operations pipeline.

1.title: Logging and monitoring, continued
1.text: Logging and monitoring. Log. A record of an event (a login, a file access, a firewall decision). Event. Any observable occurrence. Incident. An event (or events) that harms or threatens confidentiality, integrity or availability. sim. Security information and event management: collects logs from many sources, correlates them and raises alerts. Alert. A notification that something needs attention. Log the important sources: firewalls, servers, identity, applications, cloud. Visibility. Synchronize clocks (time protocol). Events line up across systems. Protect and retain logs. Evidence; attackers delete logs. Review and alert on logs. Unread logs do not protect.

1.title: Logging and monitoring, continued
1.text: Logging and monitoring. A I helps sim tools by correlating events and reducing alert fatigue; people still decide about real incidents. Exam tip: A sim collects and correlates; it does not fix. Time synchronization is needed so that logs can be correlated.

1.title: Security event triage
1.text: Security event triage. Triage is the quick sorting of alerts to decide what is real, how serious and what to do first. Validate. True positive (real attack) or false positive (harmless)? Prioritize. How severe is it, and how critical is the asset? Correlate. Do other events show a pattern (same I P, same user)? Decide. Close, escalate or start incident response.

1.title: Security event triage, continued
1.text: Security event triage. True positive. Real threat detected. False positive. Alert with no real threat. False negative. Real threat missed (the most dangerous). True negative. Normal activity, no alert. Incident use cases are scenarios the sock prepared for (for example brute force, malware beacon, impossible travel), each with detection rules and a playbook. Routine automated blocks need no action; unusual events need a human. Exam tip: Prioritize by severity and asset criticality. A false negative is worse than a false positive.

1.title: Threat actors
1.text: Threat actors. Nation-state (state-sponsored). Motivation: Espionage, sabotage, strategic advantage. Notes: Highly skilled, patient (advanced persistent threat). Organized crime. Motivation: Money: ransomware, fraud. Notes: Businesslike. Hacktivist. Motivation: Political or social cause. Notes: Defacement, leaks, D dos (distributed denial of service). Insider. Motivation: Revenge, money or mistake. Notes: Already has access. Script kiddie. Motivation: Curiosity, fame. Notes: Low skill, uses tools made by others. Competitor. Motivation: Business advantage. Notes: Industrial espionage. Exam tip: Match motive to actor: money equals crime, politics equals hacktivist, espionage equals nation-state, grievance equals insider.

1.title: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI)
1.text: Cyber threat intelligence (C T I). C T I is evidence-based knowledge about threats that helps decisions. Strategic. Audience: Executives. Content: Trends, who targets the sector. Operational. Audience: Security managers. Content: Campaigns, attacker intent. Tactical. Audience: Defenders. Content: Tactics, techniques, procedures. Technical. Audience: Tools. Content: Indicators of compromise (Io Cs): I P addresses, domains, file hashes. Sources include open-source intelligence, vendors, information sharing groups (I sacks) and government.

1.title: Threat frameworks
1.text: Threat frameworks. my ter attack. A catalog of attacker tactics and techniques, based on real observations. Cyber Kill Chain. Seven stages of an attack: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions on objectives. Diamond Model. Links adversary, capability, infrastructure and victim. stride. Threat modeling categories: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. Exam tip: attack equals what attackers do (tactics and techniques). Kill Chain equals the stages in order. stride equals a threat modeling checklist for design.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A system collects logs from firewalls, servers and applications, correlates them and raises alerts. What is it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: A sim. A security information and event management system collects, correlates and alerts.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. An alert fires for a login from an unusual country, but the employee is on a business trip. What is this alert? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: A false positive with no real threat. An alert that turns out to be harmless is a false positive.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Which result is the most dangerous for a security team? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: A false negative, where a real attack is missed. A missed real attack gives no chance to respond.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A group attacks a government agency for years to steal secrets, with high skill and patience. Which actor fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: A nation-state advanced persistent threat. Long, patient, skilled espionage is typical of a nation-state actor.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A sock receives many alerts. Which approach to triage is best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Prioritize by severity and criticality of the asset. Triage prioritizes by severity and by how critical the affected asset is.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Which framework is a catalog of attacker tactics and techniques built from real observations? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: my ter attack, a matrix of tactics and techniques. my ter attack catalogs attacker tactics and techniques seen in real attacks.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What does a sim do? Answer: Collects logs, correlates events and raises alerts. Question two. What is a false positive? Answer: An alert with no real threat. Question three. Which actor is motivated by political causes? Answer: A hacktivist.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What are indicators of compromise? Answer: Evidence such as I P addresses, domains and file hashes. Question five. How many stages does the Cyber Kill Chain have? Answer: Seven. Question six. What does the S in stride stand for? Answer: Spoofing.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Logging: sim collects and correlates; synchronize clocks; protect logs. Triage: validate, prioritize, correlate, decide; false negative is worst. Actors: nation-state, organized crime, hacktivist, insider, script kiddie. C T I: strategic, operational, tactical, technical (Io Cs). Frameworks: attack, Kill Chain (seven stages), Diamond Model, stride.
